extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of classical natural philosophy/physics and mathematics (Latin readers and historians of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and understanding Newton's foundational definitions, scholia, axioms (laws of motion), and corollaries as presented in the Principia; covers conceptual definitions of mass, motion, forces, and distinctions between absolute/relative quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics as mathematical method / approach to inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics rationalis will be the science of motions which result from forces, and of the forces required for given motions, accurately proposed and demonstrated; natural phenomena should be reduced to mathematical laws and derived from hypotheses about forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states the methodological aim: to treat natural forces (gravity, elasticity, fluid resistance, etc.) as mathematical principles, derive forces from phenomena and then deduce phenomena from these forces; prefer mathematical demonstration over purely qualitative description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. I — Quantitas Materiæ
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitas Materiæ est mensura ejusdem orta ex illius Densitate & Magnitudine conjunctim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass is measured by density and magnitude together. Mass (or quantity of matter) is understood through weight; experiments with pendulums show proportionality to weight. Note discussion that media interstitial do not change the definition here; transcriber braces clarify expressions in mathematical passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. II — Quantitas motus
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitas motus est mensura ejusdem orta ex Velocitate et quantitate Materiæ conjunctim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantity of motion (momentum) equals mass times velocity; total motion is the sum of motions of constituent parts. Examples illustrate doubling mass or velocity doubles the quantity of motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. III — Materiæ vis insita (vis inertiæ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Materiæ vis insita est potentia resistendi, qua corpus ... perseverat in statu suo vel quiescendi vel movendi uniformiter in directum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines innate force (inertia) as resistance to change of state; equates vis insita with inertia/mass conceptually. Discusses how inertia manifests as resistance to change, and differentiates Impetus and Resistentia as perspectives on the same phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. IV — Vis impressa
rubrics_metrics.description: Vis impressa est actio in corpus exercita, ad mutandum ejus statum vel quiescendi vel movendi uniformiter in directum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An impressed force is an action that alters a body's state; it is transient (does not remain in the body after action). Origins include blows, pressure, centripetal forces. Distinguish between impressed force and persistent state due to inertia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. V — Vis centripeta
rubrics_metrics.description: Vis centripeta est qua corpus versus punctum aliquod tanquam ad centrum trahitur, impellitur, vel utcunq; tendit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples: gravity, magnetic attraction, and the force causing planets to deviate from straight-line motion. Notes that centripetal force has three measures: absolute, accelerative, and motive (motrix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. VI — Vis centripetæ quantitas absoluta
rubrics_metrics.description: Vis centripetæ quantitas absoluta est mensura ejusdem major vel minor pro efficacia causæ eam propagantis a centro per regiones in circuitu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute quantity measures the inherent efficacy of the cause at the center to propagate force through surrounding regions; example: magnetic strength differing between magnets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. VII — Vis centripetæ quantitas acceleratrix
rubrics_metrics.description: Vis centripetæ quantitas acceleratrix est ipsius mensura Velocitati proporcionalis, quam dato tempore generat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accelerative measure is proportional to the velocity it generates in a given time. Examples: gravitational acceleration varying with altitude; near Earth's surface, accelerative gravity is equal for all bodies (ignoring air resistance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. VIII — Vis centripetæ quantitas motrix
rubrics_metrics.description: Vis centripetæ quantitas motrix est ipsius mensura proportionalis motui, quem dato tempore generat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motrix measure is proportional to the motion (momentum/weight) created in a body in a given time; e.g., the same accelerative force produces larger motrix effect in a more massive body (weight as measure of motrix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium — Distinction of Absolute and Relative Time
rubrics_metrics.description: Tempus absolutum verum & Mathematicum ... in se & natura sua absq; relatione ad externum quodvis, æquabiliter fluit; relativum apparens & vulgare est sensibilis & externa quævis Durationis per motum mensura.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time should be distinguished conceptually: absolute (true, mathematical) vs relative (common, apparent measured by motion—hours/days). Astronomical corrections (equation of time) and experiments (oscillating clocks, eclipses of Jupiter's satellites) illustrate the distinction and necessity of distinguishing them in astronomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium — Distinction of Absolute and Relative Space
rubrics_metrics.description: Spatium absolutum natura sua absq; relatione ad externum quodvis semper manet similare & immobile; relativum est spatii hujus mensura seu dimensio quælibet mobilis ... a vulgo pro spatio immobili usurpatur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Space absolute is immobile and of fixed nature; relative space is the measure/position of a body relative to other bodies. Examples and implications for conceptualizing motion are given, including how moving Earth would change which part of absolute space is occupied by local air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium — Definition of Locus (Place)
rubrics_metrics.description: Locus est pars spatii quam corpus occupat, estq; pro ratione spatii vel absolutus vel relativus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place is a part of space occupied by a body; differentiates locus from surface or situation. Emphasizes that loci are parts of space and have properties distinct from superficial features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium — Definition/Distinction of Absolute and Relative Motion and Quies
rubrics_metrics.description: Motus absolutus est translatio corporis de loco absoluto in locum absolutum, relativus de relativo in relativum. Quies vera est permansio corporis in eadem parte spatii illius immoti ... Quies relativa est permansio in respectu ad regionem mobilium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples (person on a ship) illustrating relative vs true motion and quies. Explains that relative measures are useful in practice but must be abstracted away in philosophical (mathematical) treatment. Discusses properties, causes, and effects distinguishing true and relative motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for inferring true motion from forces and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: True motions of bodies can be discerned from their causes and effects (e.g., tensions, forces, surface shapes). Example: two globes connected by a string rotating about their center; the string tension gives evidence of true circular motion and allows computation of its quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical method: use differences between apparent motions and true motions (forces, tensions, effects like water surface curvature) to deduce true motion even when parts of absolute space are not directly observable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lex. I — Law I (Inertia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpus omne perseverare in statu suo quiescendi vel movendi uniformiter in directum, nisi quatenus a viribus impressis cogitur statum illum mutare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objects maintain state of rest or uniform straight-line motion unless acted on by impressed forces. Examples: projectiles, trochoidal rotation, planetary motion in low-resistance spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lex. II — Law II (Change of motion proportional to impressed force)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutationem motus proportionalem esse vi motrici impressæ, & fieri secundum lineam rectam qua vis illa imprimitur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change in motion is proportional to the impressed motive force and occurs along the straight line in which the force acts. Explains vector addition of effects (concurrent and oblique additions of forces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lex. III — Law III (Action and reaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actioni contrariam semper & æqualem esse reactionem: sive corporum duorum actiones in se mutuo semper esse æquales & in partes contrarias dirigi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Examples: pressure between finger and stone, horse pulling a stone with a rope. Emphasizes equality of changes in motions (not velocities) and reciprocal effects in collisions and interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary — Parallelogram composition and resolution of forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpus viribus conjunctis diagonalem parallelogrammi eodem tempore describere, quo latera separatis ... Et hinc patet compositio vis directæ AD ex viribus quibusvis obliquis AB & BD, & vicissim resolutio vis cujusvis directæ AD in obliquas quascunq; AB & BD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the laws, shows geometric construction for composing forces (parallelogram law) and resolving a force into components; illustrated with pulleys, weights, and rotating wheel examples; underpins mechanical advantage calculations for machines (levers, pulleys, screws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary — Conservation of quantitas motus (momentum) in interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitas motus quæ colligitur ... non mutatur ab actione corporum inter se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From equal and opposite reactions and proportionality, the sum of motions in the same direction and the difference in opposite directions remain constant in mutual actions (momentum conservation). Examples with spherical bodies colliding and calculations showing post-collision motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary — Motion of the common center of gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Commune gravitatis centrum ab actionibus corporum inter se non mutat statum suum vel motus vel quietis, & propterea corporum omnium in se mutuo agentium ... commune centrum gravitatis vel quiescit vel movetur uniformiter in directum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The common center of gravity of interacting bodies is unaffected by their mutual actions (in absence of external forces) and thus either remains at rest or moves uniformly in a straight line. Demonstrated progressively for two, three, four bodies and extended to arbitrary systems.
